title: Bayesian Disease Mapping with R-INLA
text:
Some numbers rest on a lot of data, some on very little. Today we learn the Bayesian way of taking that into account, first with restaurants and a well, then with lung cancer in Pennsylvania. Reading: Moraga Ch. 3, 4 and §5.1–5.3.






NoteBy the end of today you can

explain why the SIR of a small county is unreliable;
say what shrinkage does, and to which counties;
compute a 95% credible interval by hand, and read one off a posterior curve;
read a smoothed map, credible intervals and an exceedance map made with R-INLA.

Which one would you pick? Most people pick B, even though A has the higher average: two five-star reviews could come from the owner’s friends. Without noticing, you did three things.

You started from what you know about restaurants in general: a typical one gets about 4.0 stars. That is the prior.
You looked at each restaurant’s own reviews. That is the data.
You combined the two, trusting the reviews more when there are many. That is the posterior, your best guess.

title: Bayesian Disease Mapping with R-INLA
section: The best guess is an average
text:
The best guess is an average
Where does the prior come from? Recently, 10 people tried restaurants in the area, and their average rating was 4.0 stars. We borrow these 10 ratings and add them to each restaurant’s own reviews; the best guess is the average of all the ratings, borrowed and own. With \(n\) own reviews,
\[
\text{best guess} \;=\; \frac{\text{total stars}}{\text{total ratings}}
\;=\; \frac{10 \times 4.0 \;+\; n \times \text{its average}}{10 + n}.
\]
Two or three own reviews cannot overturn the 10 borrowed ratings; a few dozen can. The same best guess is a weighted average,
\[
\text{best guess} \;=\; w \times \text{its average} \;+\; (1 - w) \times 4.0,
\qquad w = \frac{n}{n + 10},
\]
where \(w\) is the share of its own reviews: how much we trust its own reviews, between 0 and 1. In R:


Code
best_guess <- function(reviews, average, prior_mean = 4.0, borrowed = 10) {
  w <- reviews / (reviews + borrowed)           # share of its own reviews
  w * average + (1 - w) * prior_mean            # weighted average
}

best_guess(reviews = 2,   average = 5.0)        # Restaurant A


[1] 4.166667


Code
best_guess(reviews = 800, average = 4.7)        # Restaurant B


[1] 4.691358


Restaurant A’s 5.0 is pulled back to 4.17: two reviews are not enough to convince us. B barely moves, to 4.69. Pulling an estimate toward the average is called shrinkage.

title: Bayesian Disease Mapping with R-INLA
text:
2.1 The story
A family tests its well for arsenic ten times. The EPA limit is 10 µg/L. Their question: how often is this water above the limit? Call that share \(\theta\): \(\theta = 0.2\) means unsafe one test in five.


Code
epa   <- 10                                          # EPA limit, µg/L
conc  <- c(14, 7, 12, 18, 11, 15, 9, 13, 14, 14)     # 10 tests (illustrative)
above <- as.integer(conc > epa)                      # 1 = above, 0 = below
above


 [1] 1 0 1 1 1 1 0 1 1 1


We do not start from nothing. In nearby wells, about half of past tests were above the limit: 5 of 10. That is our prior, centred on \(\theta = 0.5\). A Beta curve keeps the score: Beta(5, 5) means 5 tests above and 5 below, borrowed from the neighbours. Each new test above the limit adds 1 to the first number, each test below adds 1 to the second.

title: Bayesian Disease Mapping with R-INLA
text:
2.2 Watching the posterior learn
In each panel, red dotted is what we believed before the test, green is what we believe after.


Code
plot_update <- function(a, b, x, n, title = "") {
  theta <- seq(0, 1, 0.001)
  plot(theta, dbeta(theta, a, b), type = "l", lty = 3, lwd = 3, col = "red",
       ylim = c(0, 4), bty = "l", xlab = expression(theta), ylab = "",
       main = title)                                            # before
  if (n > 0)                                                    # no test, no update
    lines(theta, dbeta(theta, a + x, b + n - x), lwd = 3, col = "darkgreen")  # after
}




Code
par(mfrow = c(3, 4), mar = c(4, 2, 2, 1))

a <- 5; b <- 5                                      # prior: 5 of 10 above in nearby wells
plot_update(a, b, 0, 0, title = "Before testing: nearby wells")

for (i in 1:10) {
  plot_update(a, b, above[i], 1,
              title = paste0("#", i, ": ", conc[i], " ug/L",
                             ifelse(above[i] == 1, " (above)", " (below)")))
  a <- a + above[i]                                 # after ...
  b <- b + 1 - above[i]                             # ... becomes next before
}








Figure 2: Each panel starts from the previous panel’s green curve and adds one test.





Three things to notice:

A test above the limit pushes the curve right; a test below pushes it left (tests 2 and 7).
The curve gets taller and narrower: more tests, more certainty.
Each panel’s green curve becomes the next panel’s red curve. That is Bayesian learning.







Note



Why does the y-axis stop at 4? It shows a density, not a probability, so it can exceed 1; the area under each curve is 1. We fix it at 4 so the panels can be compared.

section: 2.3 What do we know after ten tests?
text:
2.3 What do we know after ten tests?


Code
a / (a + b)                                      # best guess for θ


[1] 0.65


Code
qbeta(c(0.025, 0.975), a, b)                     # 95% credible interval


[1] 0.4344984 0.8371141


Code
1 - pbeta(0.5, a, b)                             # P(unsafe more than half the time)


[1] 0.9164658


Our best guess is that the water is above the limit about 65% of the time, and with 95% probability between 43% and 84% (the credible interval). The probability that it is unsafe more than half the time is 0.92. Bayesian results answer the family’s question directly, as a probability.
Where does 65% come from? The well’s own tests say 8 of 10, 80%. The nearby wells say 50%. The prior is worth 10 tests and the well has 10 of its own, so the answer sits halfway. It is the restaurant formula again:
\[
0.65 \;=\; w \times 0.80
\;+\; (1 - w) \times 0.50,
\qquad w = \frac{10}{10 + 10} = 0.5.
\]






TipKey idea



We start from what we already know, here the nearby wells, and each new test updates it. More data, a narrower curve, more certainty.

title: Bayesian Disease Mapping with R-INLA
text:
3.4 The funnel plot
How far can an SIR stray by chance alone? If a county’s true risk were exactly the state’s, its SIR would still fall, about 95% of the time, within \(1 \pm 1.96/\sqrt{E}\). Plotted against \(E\), that range is a funnel.


Code
funnel <- tibble(E = exp(seq(log(4), log(1500), length.out = 200))) |>
  mutate(lo = 1 - 1.96 / sqrt(E),                   # chance range of the SIR
         hi = 1 + 1.96 / sqrt(E))

labelled <- filter(county, county %in% c("sullivan", "potter", "juniata", "philadelphia"))

ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = funnel, aes(E, ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "grey85") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(data = county, aes(E, SIR)) +
  geom_text(data = labelled, aes(E, SIR, label = tools::toTitleCase(county)),
            nudge_y = 0.07, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Expected cases (log scale)", y = "SIR") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)








Figure 4: SIRs against expected cases. Grey: where about 95% of SIRs fall by chance alone.





The funnel is wide on the left. Potter’s 1.37 and Sullivan’s 0.40 sit inside it: they could be chance. Philadelphia’s 1.16 is far outside: with more than 1,200 expected cases, a 16% excess is not chance.






ImportantThe problem in one sentence



A raw SIR mixes real differences in risk with chance, and chance is largest in small counties.

title: Bayesian Disease Mapping with R-INLA
text:
4.2 Who decides \(k\)? The data
For the restaurants we picked 10 ourselves. For counties, R estimates \(k\) from the 67 SIRs:

if counties differ much more than chance alone would produce, real differences are large, the state average is worth little, and \(k\) is small;
if counties differ about as much as chance would produce, the state average is worth a lot, and \(k\) is large.

Letting the data choose the prior this way is called empirical Bayes (Clayton and Kaldor 1987; Marshall 1991). EBest() in spdep does it in one line.


Code
eb <- EBest(pa$O, pa$E)                              # cases, expected cases
pa$RR_eb <- eb$estmm                                 # shrunk estimate

k <- with(attr(eb, "parameters"), b / a)             # state worth k expected cases
k

title: Bayesian Disease Mapping with R-INLA
section: How does INLA get a credible interval?
text:
How does INLA get a credible interval?
For every county, INLA returns a whole posterior curve for its relative risk, like the green curves of the well. For the well, a simple formula gave the curve. Here it cannot, because each county borrows from its neighbours, and we do not know how much to borrow: that depends on how different the counties really are, which is itself unknown. INLA works in three steps (Moraga §3.2):

Try several amounts of borrowing. For each plausible value of how much the counties differ, it computes the county’s curve with a fast bell-shaped (Laplace) approximation.
Average the curves. It weights each curve by how well that amount of borrowing fits all 67 counties, and averages them. This is the integrated in INLA.
Read the final curve. The posterior mean is its balance point; the 95% credible interval cuts 2.5% of the area off each side; the exceedance probability is the area to the right of 1.

Here are steps 1 and 2 for Potter. Each dashed curve fixes one amount of borrowing, from little to a lot; the thick grey curve is INLA’s final curve.


Code
k   <- which(dat$county == "potter")
tau <- c(10, m2$summary.hyperpar["Precision for id", "0.5quant"], 1000)   # little, middle, a lot
phi <- m2$summary.hyperpar["Phi for id", "0.5quant"]

fixed_fit <- function(t) {                           # BYM2 with borrowing fixed
  hyp <- list(prec = list(initial = log(t),   fixed = TRUE),
              phi  = list(initial = qlogis(phi), fixed = TRUE))
  m <- inla(O ~ 1 + f(id, model = "bym2", graph = g, hyper = hyp),
            family = "poisson", E = E, data = dat,
            control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
            control.compute = list(return.marginals.predictor = TRUE))
  inla.smarginal(m$marginals.fitted.values[[k]])     # Potter's curve
}

lab <- c("borrow little (counties very different)", "borrow a middle amount",
         "borrow a lot (counties very similar)")
steps <- bind_rows(lapply(1:3, function(j) data.frame(fixed_fit(tau[j]), curve = lab[j]))) |>
  mutate(curve = factor(curve, lab))
final <- data.frame(inla.smarginal(m2$marginals.fitted.values[[k]]))

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = final, aes(x, y), linewidth = 2.5, alpha = 0.35) +     # final curve, underneath
  geom_line(data = steps, aes(x, y, colour = curve), linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = dat$SIR[k], linetype = 3, colour = "blue") +
  annotate("text", x = dat$SIR[k], y = 0, label = " Potter's SIR", hjust = 0,
           vjust = -0.5, colour = "blue", size = 3.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#D95F02", "#7570B3", "#1B9E77"), name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.5, 1.8)) +
  labs(x = "Relative risk, Potter", y = "Posterior density") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.direction = "vertical")








Figure 6: Potter County. Dashed: posterior curves for three fixed amounts of borrowing. Thick grey: INLA’s final curve, which averages over all plausible amounts.





Borrowing little leaves Potter closer to its own SIR, with a wide curve; borrowing a lot pulls it toward its neighbours, with a narrow curve. The data make the middle amount the most plausible, so the final curve sits close to it. Step 3 then reads the answers off the final curve:


Code
LL <- m2$summary.fitted.values$`0.025quant`[k]
UL <- m2$summary.fitted.values$`0.975quant`[k]
P1 <- 1 - inla.pmarginal(1, m2$marginals.fitted.values[[k]])

p_ci <- ggplot(final, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(final, x <= LL), fill = "grey70") +
  geom_area(data = filter(final, x >= UL), fill = "grey70") +
  geom_line(colour = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(LL, UL), linetype = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = UL + 0.04, y = max(final$y) * 0.6, size = 3.5, hjust = 0,
           label = paste0("95% credible interval\n", sprintf("%.2f", LL),
                          " to ", sprintf("%.2f", UL))) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.5, 1.8)) +
  labs(title = "Credible interval", x = "Relative risk, Potter", y = "Posterior density") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)

p_exc <- ggplot(final, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(final, x >= 1), fill = "#d7191c", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(colour = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.35, y = max(final$y) * 0.6, size = 3.5,
           label = paste0("P(risk > 1) = ", sprintf("%.2f", P1))) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.5, 1.8)) +
  labs(title = "Exceedance probability", x = "Relative risk, Potter", y = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)

p_ci + p_exc








Figure 7: Potter’s final posterior curve. Left: the 95% credible interval leaves 2.5% of the area in each grey tail. Right: the exceedance probability is the red area to the right of 1.

section: 5.5 How sure are we? The exceedance map
text:
5.5 How sure are we? The exceedance map
For the well we asked: how likely is it that the water is unsafe more than half the time? For each county we ask: how likely is it that its risk is above the state average, \(P(\theta > 1)\)? This is the exceedance probability: the area of the posterior curve to the right of 1. A county whose whole 95% credible interval is above 1 has \(P(\theta > 1) > 0.975\).


Code
dat$p_exc <- sapply(m2$marginals.fitted.values,
                    function(m) 1 - inla.pmarginal(1, m))   # P(θ > 1)




Code
exc_cols <- c("Probably lower (< 0.2)"  = "#2c7bb6",
              "Uncertain (0.2–0.8)"     = "grey90",
              "Probably higher (> 0.8)" = "#d7191c")

pa |>
  select(county) |>
  left_join(select(dat, county, p_exc), by = "county") |>
  mutate(exc = cut(p_exc, c(0, 0.2, 0.8, 1), labels = names(exc_cols),
                   include.lowest = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = exc), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = exc_cols, drop = FALSE, name = NULL) +
  theme_void(base_size = 12)








Figure 14: Probability that each county’s lung cancer risk exceeds the state average (BYM2).





Counties probably above average: Allegheny, Bucks, Butler, Delaware, Philadelphia, Venango. Potter, despite its SIR of 1.37, is not among them (\(P = 0.38\)): 22 cases are not enough.






TipKey idea



INLA does the same shrinkage, borrows from the neighbours, and tells us how sure we are about each county.

Two or three own reviews cannot overturn the 10 borrowed ratings; a few dozen can. The same best guess is a weighted average,
\[
\text{best guess} \;=\; w \times \text{its average} \;+\; (1 - w) \times 4.0,
\qquad w = \frac{n}{n + 10},
\]
where \(w\) is the share of its own reviews: how much we trust its own reviews, between 0 and 1. In R:


Code
best_guess <- function(reviews, average, prior_mean = 4.0, borrowed = 10) {
  w <- reviews / (reviews + borrowed)           # share of its own reviews
  w * average + (1 - w) * prior_mean            # weighted average
}

title: Bayesian Disease Mapping with R-INLA
text:
The story
A family tests its well for arsenic ten times. The EPA limit is 10 µg/L. Their question: how often is this water above the limit? Call that share \(\theta\): \(\theta = 0.2\) means unsafe one test in five.


Code
epa   <- 10                                          # EPA limit, µg/L
conc  <- c(14, 7, 12, 18, 11, 15, 9, 13, 14, 14)     # 10 tests (illustrative)
above <- as.integer(conc > epa)                      # 1 = above, 0 = below
above


 [1] 1 0 1 1 1 1 0 1 1 1


We do not start from nothing. In nearby wells, about half of past tests were above the limit: 5 of 10. That is our prior, centred on \(\theta = 0.5\). A Beta curve keeps the score: Beta(5, 5) means 10 tests borrowed from the neighbours, 5 above and 5 below. Each new test above the limit adds 1 to the first number, each test below adds 1 to the second.

title: Bayesian Disease Mapping with R-INLA
text:
Watching the posterior learn
In each panel, red dotted is what we believed before the test, green is what we believe after.


Code
plot_update <- function(a, b, x, n, title = "") {
  theta <- seq(0, 1, 0.001)
  plot(theta, dbeta(theta, a, b), type = "l", lty = 3, lwd = 3, col = "red",
       ylim = c(0, 4), bty = "l", xlab = expression(theta), ylab = "",
       main = title)                                            # before
  if (n > 0)                                                    # no test, no update
    lines(theta, dbeta(theta, a + x, b + n - x), lwd = 3, col = "darkgreen")  # after
}




Code
par(mfrow = c(3, 4), mar = c(4, 2, 2, 1))

a <- 5; b <- 5                                      # prior: 5 of 10 above in nearby wells
plot_update(a, b, 0, 0, title = "Before testing: nearby wells")

for (i in 1:10) {
  plot_update(a, b, above[i], 1,
              title = paste0("#", i, ": ", conc[i], " ug/L",
                             ifelse(above[i] == 1, " (above)", " (below)")))
  a <- a + above[i]                                 # after ...
  b <- b + 1 - above[i]                             # ... becomes next before
}








Figure 2: Each panel starts from the previous panel’s green curve and adds one test.





Three things to notice:

A test above the limit pushes the curve right; a test below pushes it left (tests 2 and 7).
The curve gets taller and narrower: more tests, more certainty.
Each panel’s green curve becomes the next panel’s red curve. That is Bayesian learning.







Note



Why does the y-axis stop at 4? It shows a density, not a probability, so it can exceed 1; the area under each curve is 1. We fix it at 4 so the panels can be compared.

\;+\; (1 - w) \times 0.50,
\qquad w = \frac{10}{10 + 10} = 0.5.

title: Bayesian Disease Mapping with R-INLA
text:
Who decides \(k\)? The data
For the restaurants we picked 10 ourselves. For counties, R estimates \(k\) from the 67 SIRs:

if counties differ much more than chance alone would produce, real differences are large, we trust each county’s SIR, and \(k\) is small;
if counties differ about as much as chance would produce, we trust the state average more, and \(k\) is large.

Letting the data choose the prior this way is called empirical Bayes (Clayton and Kaldor 1987; Marshall 1991). EBest() in spdep does it in one line.

title: Empirical Bayes Disease Mapping in Pennsylvania
text:
One simple formula
A global empirical Bayes estimate is a weighted average of the county’s raw SIR and the overall Pennsylvania reference:
\[
\widehat\theta_i = w_i\,\mathrm{SIR}_i + (1-w_i)\,m,
\qquad
w_i = \frac{a}{a + m/E_i}.
\]

\(m\): overall reference (approximately 1 because the expected counts were calculated using Pennsylvania rates);
\(a\): estimated between-county variation;
\(w_i\): weight placed on the county’s own SIR, between 0 and 1.

When \(E_i\) is small, \(w_i\) tends to be smaller and the county’s SIR moves more toward the statewide reference. The data determine \(a\) and \(m\); we do not choose arbitrary weights.

title: Empirical Bayes Disease Mapping in Pennsylvania
text:
Run global empirical Bayes

# Counts (O) and expected cases (E) give smoothed relative risks.
eb_global <- EBest(pa$O, pa$E, family = "poisson")
pa$RR_global <- eb_global$estmm

# In the Poisson implementation, parameters are called 'a' and 'b'.
# 'b' is the overall reference m; 'a' is between-county variation.
par_global <- attr(eb_global, "parameters")
a_global <- par_global$a
m_global <- par_global$b

# Weight on the county's observed SIR.
pa$w_global <- a_global / (a_global + m_global / pa$E)

# Confirm the weighted-average formula reproduces EBest() results.
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
  unname(pa$RR_global),
  unname(pa$w_global * pa$SIR + (1 - pa$w_global) * m_global),
  tolerance = 1e-7
)))

section: 1.2 The best guess is a weighted average
text:
1.2 The best guess is a weighted average
Say our prior is worth 10 reviews of 4.0 stars. The best guess for a restaurant is
\[
\text{best guess} \;=\; w \times \text{its average} \;+\; (1 - w) \times 4.0,
\qquad w = \frac{\text{its reviews}}{\text{its reviews} + 10}.
\]
\(w\) is how much we trust its own reviews, between 0 and 1. In R:


Code
best_guess <- function(reviews, average, prior_mean = 4.0, prior_worth = 10) {
  w <- reviews / (reviews + prior_worth)        # trust in its own reviews
  w * average + (1 - w) * prior_mean            # weighted average
}

[1] 4.166667

section: 4.4 From one number to a whole curve
text:
4.4 From one number to a whole curve
Empirical Bayes gives one number per county, but behind it is a whole curve, as for the well. The state average, worth \(k \approx\) 108 expected cases, is the prior: a curve centred on 1 (red, dotted). The county’s own \(O\) cases for \(E\) expected are the data (blue). The posterior combines the two (green). Its centre, the best guess, is the empirical Bayes estimate, \((k + O)/(k + E)\). The middle 95% of its area, shaded, is the 95% credible interval: the county’s true risk lies in it with 95% probability.


Code
three <- county |>
  filter(county %in% c("sullivan", "potter", "philadelphia")) |>
  mutate(w          = E / (E + k),                      # trust in own SIR
         best_guess = (k + O) / (k + E),                # = empirical Bayes
         CI_low     = qgamma(0.025, k + O, k + E),      # 95% credible interval
         CI_high    = qgamma(0.975, k + O, k + E)) |>
  arrange(E)

three |>
  mutate(across(c(E, SIR, w, best_guess, CI_low, CI_high), \(x) round(x, 2)))

         Prior     = dgamma(theta, k, k),                # state, worth k cases
         Data      = dgamma(theta, x$O + 1, x$E),        # own cases only
         Posterior = dgamma(theta, k + x$O, k + x$E),    # both together

}

Potter’s SIR of 1.37 is pulled back to 1.05, and its interval, 0.88 to 1.24, contains 1: we cannot say that Potter’s risk is above the state’s. title: Bayesian Disease Mapping with R-INLA
text:
4.5 The credible interval by hand
The posterior curve above is set by two numbers:
\[
a = k + O \;\;\text{(borrowed + own cases)}, \qquad
b = k + E \;\;\text{(borrowed + own expected cases)}.
\]
With a calculator, four steps give the 95% credible interval:



Step
Formula




1. best guess
\(a / b\)


2. spread (standard deviation)
\(\sqrt{a} \,/\, b\)


3. low end
best guess \(- \, 1.96 \times\) spread


4. high end
best guess \(+ \, 1.96 \times\) spread



This is the familiar “estimate \(\pm\) 1.96 standard errors”, applied to the posterior. R’s qgamma() instead cuts exactly 2.5% of the area off each side of the curve. Both, for Sullivan:


Code
su     <- filter(county, county == "sullivan")
a      <- k + su$O                                  # borrowed + own cases
b      <- k + su$E                                  # borrowed + own expected
best   <- a / b                                     # step 1
spread <- sqrt(a) / b                               # step 2
round(c(a = a, b = b, best_guess = best, spread = spread), 3)


         a          b best_guess     spread 
   110.908    115.328      0.962      0.091 


Code
round(best + c(-1.96, 1.96) * spread, 2)            # steps 3-4: by hand


[1] 0.78 1.14


Code
round(qgamma(c(0.025, 0.975), a, b), 2)             # exact: cut 2.5% each side


[1] 0.79 1.15




Code
ex   <- qgamma(c(0.025, 0.975), a, b)               # exact interval
hand <- best + c(-1.96, 1.96) * spread              # by hand
d    <- tibble(x = seq(best - 5 * spread, best + 5 * spread, length.out = 600),
               y = dgamma(x, a, b))
top  <- max(d$y)

ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(d, x <= ex[1]), fill = "grey70") +                 # lower 2.5%
  geom_area(data = filter(d, x >= ex[2]), fill = "grey70") +                 # upper 2.5%
  geom_area(data = filter(d, x >= ex[1], x <= ex[2]), fill = "darkgreen", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(colour = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best, colour = "darkgreen", linetype = 2) +         # best guess
  annotate("text", x = c(ex[1] - 0.6 * spread, best + 0.9 * spread, ex[2] + 0.6 * spread),
           y = top * c(0.12, 0.45, 0.12), label = c("2.5%", "95%", "2.5%")) +
  annotate("segment", x = hand[1], xend = hand[2], y = -0.12 * top,
           yend = -0.12 * top, linewidth = 1.2) +                            # by hand
  annotate("text", x = best, y = -0.22 * top, size = 3.5,
           label = "by hand: best guess +/- 1.96 x spread") +
  labs(x = "Relative risk, Sullivan County", y = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)








Figure 7: Sullivan’s posterior. Grey: the 2.5% cut off on each side. Green: the middle 95%, the exact credible interval. Black bar: the interval by hand.





Here \(a\) is large, about 111, so the curve is almost symmetric and the two intervals agree to about 0.01. When a county borrows little, the curve is lopsided and the interval by hand is only an approximation; you will see this in Exercise 7.






TipKey idea



A credible interval is read off the posterior curve: cut 2.5% of the area on each side. By hand, best guess \(\pm\) 1.96 \(\times\) spread comes close.

5.4 Borrowing from the neighbours
Empirical Bayes pulls every county toward the state average. BYM2 pulls it mostly toward its neighbours. Potter, outlined in black, and its neighbours:


Code
i    <- which(dat$county == "potter")
hood <- pa[c(i, nb[[i]]), ]                          # Potter, then its neighbours

p_map <- ggplot(hood) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cut(SIR, sir_breaks)), colour = "white") +
  geom_sf(data = hood[1, ], fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 1) +   # Potter
  geom_sf_text(aes(label = paste0(tc(county), "\n", sprintf("%.2f", SIR))),
               size = 3) +
  sir_fill +
  labs(title = "Raw SIRs") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

          "Potter, empirical Bayes", "Potter, BYM2 best guess")

              value = c(hood$SIR[-1], 1, dat$SIR[i], dat$RR_eb[i], dat$RR_bym2[i]))
bar <- tibble(what = factor(rows[5], rev(rows)), lo = dat$LL[i], hi = dat$UL[i])

p_line <- ggplot(pts, aes(value, what, colour = what)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_linerange(data = bar, aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi, y = what), inherit.aes = FALSE,

section: 2.1 What we want: a curve, not a number
text:
2.1 What we want: a curve, not a number
A Bayesian model returns, for each county, a whole posterior curve: which relative risks are plausible, and how plausible. There are two ways to get it.


Code
a <- 8; b <- 7                                     # an illustrative posterior
set.seed(374)

hist_panel <- function(n) {
  ggplot(tibble(x = rgamma(n, a, b)), aes(x)) +
    geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 0.1, boundary = 0,
                   fill = "grey60", colour = "white") +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 3), ylim = c(0, 1.8)) +
    labs(title = paste0("MCMC: ", format(n, big.mark = ","), " draws"),
         x = "Relative risk", y = NULL) +
    theme_classic(base_size = 11)
}

p_inla <- ggplot(tibble(x = seq(0, 3, 0.01)), aes(x, dgamma(x, a, b))) +
  geom_area(fill = "darkgreen", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(colour = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 3), ylim = c(0, 1.8)) +
  labs(title = "INLA: the curve", x = "Relative risk", y = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 11)

hist_panel(100) + hist_panel(5000) + p_inla








Figure 2: Same posterior, two routes. MCMC draws random values and builds a histogram; INLA computes the curve.





MCMC is like a poll: draw thousands of plausible values and count them. It works for almost any model, but it is slow, and you must check that it drew enough. INLA skips the drawing and computes the curve with an approximation. For disease maps it takes seconds, and its curves are usually very close to MCMC’s (Rue et al. 2009).

title: INLA, BYM and BYM2 in Pictures
section: 2.2 The trick: a bell curve at the top
text:
2.2 The trick: a bell curve at the top


Code
peak  <- (a - 1) / b                               # top of the curve
width <- sqrt(a - 1) / b                           # width at the top

tibble(x = seq(0, 3, 0.01),
       `True curve`     = dgamma(x, a, b),
       `Bell (Laplace)` = dnorm(x, peak, width)) |>
  pivot_longer(-x, names_to = "curve", values_to = "density") |>
  ggplot(aes(x, density, colour = curve, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = peak, colour = "grey60", linetype = 3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("True curve" = "darkgreen", "Bell (Laplace)" = "darkorange")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("True curve" = 1, "Bell (Laplace)" = 2)) +
  labs(x = "Relative risk", y = NULL, colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")








Figure 3: The Laplace approximation: a bell curve with the same peak and the same width at the top.





Close, not exact. INLA works on the log scale, where curves are closer to a bell, and then corrects the bell. The name says the rest:








Letters
Stands for
In plain words




I
Integrated
averages over the few unknown settings of the model, e.g. how smooth the map is


N
Nested
approximations inside approximations: first those settings, then each county


LA
Laplace Approximation
a bell curve fitted at the top of each curve, then refined









TipKey idea



You never see any of this. You write a formula; INLA returns one curve per county. Today only the model = ... part of the formula changes.

title: INLA, BYM and BYM2 in Pictures
text:
4.1 Neighbours map and noise map
BYM (Besag, York and Mollié 1991) says the log-risk of county \(i\) is an overall level plus two hidden maps:
\[
\log \theta_i \;=\; \beta_0 \;+\; \underbrace{u_i}_{\text{neighbours}} \;+\; \underbrace{v_i}_{\text{noise}}
\]
What do these two maps look like before we see any data? Here is one random draw of each.


Code
W <- nb2mat(nb, style = "B")                       # 1 = neighbours
Q <- diag(rowSums(W)) - 0.99 * W                   # nearly the ICAR (Besag) prior
set.seed(374)
u_sim <- as.vector(scale(backsolve(chol(Q), rnorm(nrow(pa)))))   # smooth map
v_sim <- as.vector(scale(rnorm(nrow(pa))))                       # pure noise

map_effect(u_sim, "u: neighbours look alike", lim = 2.5) +
  map_effect(v_sim, "v: every county for itself", lim = 2.5) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect")








Figure 5: Left: u, a smooth map where neighbours look alike (structured). Right: v, pure county-to-county noise (unstructured). Simulated.





A real map is a mix of both. BYM lets the data decide how much of each.

title: INLA, BYM and BYM2 in Pictures
text:
4.2 Fitting BYM


Code
dat$idu <- dat$id                                  # one index per f() term
dat$idv <- dat$id

m_bym <- inla(O ~ 1 + f(idu, model = "besag", graph = g) +   # u: neighbours
                      f(idv, model = "iid"),                 # v: noise
              family = "poisson", E = E, data = dat,
              control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
              control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE))

b0         <- m_bym$summary.fixed["(Intercept)", "mean"]   # overall level
dat$u      <- m_bym$summary.random$idu$mean                # neighbours map
dat$v      <- m_bym$summary.random$idv$mean                # noise map
dat$RR_bym <- m_bym$summary.fitted.values$mean             # relative risk


Writing BYM as two f() terms shows its two pieces. INLA also offers it in one piece, model = "bym".

title: INLA, BYM and BYM2 in Pictures
section: 4.3 The BYM map as an addition
text:
4.3 The BYM map as an addition


Code
lim <- max(abs(c(b0, dat$u, dat$v)))               # one scale for the pieces

map_effect(rep(b0, nrow(pa)), "Overall level", lim) +
  map_effect(dat$u, "+ u (neighbours)", lim) +
  map_effect(dat$v, "+ v (noise)", lim) +
  map_risk(exp(b0 + dat$u + dat$v), "= relative risk") +
  plot_layout(nrow = 1, guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 6: Pennsylvania’s BYM map, piece by piece. The first three maps share one colour scale.





Read it left to right. The overall level is the same everywhere. Then each county gets a bump from its neighbourhood (\(u\)) and a bump of its own (\(v\)). Because the three pieces share one scale, the stronger colours show which hidden map carries more of Pennsylvania’s pattern.






WarningThe catch with BYM



BYM has two knobs: how much \(u\) varies and how much \(v\) varies. They are hard to read, and they compete: the data cannot easily tell which map should carry a pattern, so the two knobs are hard to estimate and to set priors for (Riebler et al. 2016). BYM2 replaces them with two knobs that mean something.

title: INLA, BYM and BYM2 in Pictures
text:
5.1 Turning the knob
BYM2 keeps the same two hidden maps and mixes them:
\[
\log \theta_i \;=\; \beta_0 \;+\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau}}
\Big(\sqrt{\phi}\;u_i^{*} \;+\; \sqrt{1-\phi}\;v_i\Big)
\]
\(u^*\) is \(u\) rescaled to the same typical size as \(v\). Then \(\tau\) says how much counties differ, and \(\phi\), between 0 and 1, says how spatial the differences are. Here is the knob, on the two simulated maps from above:


Code
phis <- c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)

knob <- lapply(phis, function(p) {
  map_effect(sqrt(p) * u_sim + sqrt(1 - p) * v_sim,   # BYM2 mix
             bquote(phi == .(p)), lim = 2.5) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
})

wrap_plots(knob, nrow = 1)








Figure 7: Mixing the same two maps with φ. Left: all noise. Right: all neighbours. Every panel has the same total variation.





Only the shape of the map changes with \(\phi\), not how much it varies. That is why \(\phi\) is easy to read: the share of the variation that is spatial.

text:
5.3 Where does Pennsylvania sit on the knob?


Code
phi_curve <- inla.smarginal(m_bym2$marginals.hyperpar$`Phi for id`)   # INLA's curve
phi_mean  <- m_bym2$summary.hyperpar["Phi for id", "mean"]
phi_ci    <- unlist(m_bym2$summary.hyperpar["Phi for id", c("0.025quant", "0.975quant")])

ggplot(as.data.frame(phi_curve), aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(fill = "purple", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(colour = "purple", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = phi_mean, colour = "purple", linetype = 2) +
  annotate("label", x = c(0, 1), y = 0, label = c("all noise", "all neighbours"),
           hjust = c(0, 1), vjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = expression(paste(phi, ", share of the variation that is spatial")), y = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)








Figure 8: Posterior curve of φ for lung cancer in Pennsylvania. Dashed: posterior mean.





The posterior mean of \(\phi\) is 0.53, with 95% probability between 0.10 and 0.93. In the knob figure, Pennsylvania sits closest to the panel \(\phi\) = 0.5. BYM could only hint at this by comparing colours; BYM2 gives it as one number, with its uncertainty.
